direct_claims: This chart compares how participants answered whether specific popular apps have OSIs, using three response categories: yes, not sure, and no.
The bars are normalized to percentages, so each app is compared by response distribution rather than by raw sample size alone.
The chart shows the top 15 most popular apps, defined as apps used by at least 10% of participants.
The source context is a CHI 2020 paper, which places the figure in human-computer interaction research rather than product marketing or app analytics.
A key takeaway stated in the title and expert story is that participants recognized OSIs in Discord more often, while only a few knew that MyFitnessPal had them.
In this research context, the chart is measuring user awareness of whether an app includes OSIs, not whether the app is popular or whether participants approve of the feature.
Because each bar is scaled to 100%, the chart is best interpreted as a comparison of awareness patterns within each app’s respondents rather than a comparison of total respondent volume across apps.
The expert story suggests that differences across apps may be related to how OSIs are designed in each app.
The Instagram example is especially important: OSIs there are only visible between users of the messaging feature, so awareness may depend on whether a participant actually uses that part of the app.

The metadata also mentions a separate Table 4 comparing a green dot experimental condition with other colors, but no values from that table are provided here, so no reliable statistical claims about that comparison can be made from the supplied materials.
Because the underlying numeric table is absent, exact percentages for each response category should be treated as approximate unless extracted directly from the image.
